newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EP to reject changes to EU banana regime.
newsitem.headline: EP to reject changes to EU banana regime.

text.p: The European Union must not cut the quantity of bananas which former European colonies are allowed to export to the EU market, the European Parliament is expected to say next week.
"We can't accept a change, both on principle and for technical reasons," Euro-MP Giacomo Santini told Reuters on Wednesday.

Santini, the author of a report on the EU's banana import regime, rejects the European Commission's proposal to cut from 30 to 26 percent the share of the banana tariff quota allotted to traditional suppliers from Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific (ACP).

In March this year, Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler proposed increasing the overall tariff quota from 2.2 million tonnes to 2.553 million, to account for the accession of Austria, Finland and Sweden -- COM(96)82.
At the same time, he proposed raising from 66.5 to 70.5 percent the share of the market allotted to suppliers of Latin American bananas -- mainly U.S.-based multinationals .
This extra four percent was to come from operators marketing fruit from the less competitive ACP states.

The planned switch, which has yet to win the approval of ministers, leaves more or less unaltered the actual quantity of bananas the ACP states can export to the EU (a rise from 660,000 to 663,000 tonnes).
There is little practical sense in increasing the ACP quota because the ACP producers do not have the capacity to supply any more bananas, a Commission official told Reuters.
In support of the change, the Commission has also argued that only Latin American (or "dollar") bananas are marketed in the three new EU member states.
But these arguments do not wash with the parliament, which is due to demand on December 12 a reversal of the changes.
"We won't change just because the big multinationals want it," Santini, a Union for Europe group member, said, adding that the ACP producers had sought parliament support.

The Commission's argument that the new member states only import dollar bananas is "an absurd assertion which runs counter to a single market and a common market organisation," according to the Italian's report.

In addition, the Commission's proposal undermines the EU's commitment, enshrined in a protocol on bananas, to ensure that conditions imposed on ACP states should never be worse than those obtaining in the past, Santini argues.
"The 30 percent tariff quota volume amounts to the minimum compensation required in order to guarantee their survival and offer any sort of prospects for the future," his report continues.
Santini argues that the EU banana market is already saturated and that the planned 353,000-tonne rise in the tariff quota is excessive.
Since the June 1995 price slump ACP producers, who have high production costs, have been unable to break even.
Hikes in the tariff quota should therefore be restricted to a minimum, Santini believes.
